q: Who were Xun Yu's sons, and what offices did each of them hold?
reply:
## Xun Yu's Sons and Their Offices

According to the *Sanguozhi* (Wei section, "Xun Yu, Xun You, Jia Xu" chapter), Xun Yu had the following sons:

**1. Xun Yun 荀恽 (the eldest, courtesy name Changqian 长倩)** — the main text states:

> 「子惲，嗣侯，官至虎賁中郎將。」[3]
> *"His son Yun inherited the marquisate and rose to the office of 虎賁中郎將 (General of the Household Gentlemen of the Tiger Guard)."*

He was Xun Yu's eldest son and married Cao Cao's daughter, later called Princess Anyang: 「太祖以女妻彧長子惲，後稱安陽公主」[7]. He died young.

**2. Xun Yu 荀俁 (courtesy name Shuqian 叔倩)** — 
> 「惲弟俁，御史中丞」[3]
> *"Yun's younger brother Yu was 御史中丞 (Palace Assistant Secretary / Chief Censor)."*

**3. Xun Shen 荀诜 (courtesy name Manqian 曼倩)** — 
> 「俁弟詵，大將軍從事中郎，皆知名，早卒」[3]
> *"Yu's younger brother Shen was 大將軍從事中郎 (Attendant Officer of the Great General); both were well known and died young."*

**4. Xun Yi 荀顗 (courtesy name Jingqian 景倩)** — 
> 「詵弟顗，咸熙中爲司空」[3]
> *"Shen's younger brother Yi became 司空 (Minister of Works) in the Xianxi era."*

Pei's commentary, citing the *Jinyangqiu* (《晉陽秋》), adds more detail: 「擢拜散騎侍郎。顗佐命晉室，位至太尉，封臨淮康公」[6] — *"He was promoted to 散騎侍郎 (Attendant Cavalier), assisted in founding the Jin house, and reached the office of 太尉 (Grand Commandant), enfeoffed as Duke Kang of Linhuai."*

**5. Xun Can 荀粲 (courtesy name Fengqian 奉倩)** — this son appears only in Pei's commentary, cited from the *Jinyangqiu* / He Shao's biography of him:

> 「顗弟粲，字奉倩……又論父彧不如從兄攸。」[6]
> *"Yi's younger brother Can, courtesy name Fengqian… he also argued that his father Yu was inferior to his elder cousin You."*

The note expressly calls Xun Yu his 「父彧」[6], confirming he was Xun Yu's son. **No office is recorded for him** — he was known as a pure Daoist conversationalist, married a daughter of the cavalry general Cao Hong, and died at twenty-nine: 「痛悼不能已，歳餘亦亡，時年二十九」[18].

### Summary table

| Son | Courtesy name | Office(s) recorded |
|---|---|---|
| Xun Yun 荀恽 | 长倩 | Inherited the marquisate; 虎賁中郎將 [3]; married Princess Anyang [7] |
| Xun Yu 荀俁 | 叔倩 | 御史中丞 [3] |
| Xun Shen 荀诜 | 曼倩 | 大將軍從事中郎 [3] |
| Xun Yi 荀顗 | 景倩 | 司空 (Xianxi era) [3]; 散騎侍郎, later 太尉, Duke Kang of Linhuai [6] |
| Xun Can 荀粲 | 奉倩 | none recorded [6][18] |

### Notes and inference

- The four sons named in Chen Shou's main text (Yun, Yu, Shen, Yi) are the ones the *Sanguozhi* proper lists; **Xun Can appears only in Pei's supplementary notes**, so a reader relying on the main text alone would miss him. Based on this, I infer the family had at least five sons.
- The main text does not state the birth order beyond calling Xun Yun the eldest (「彧長子惲」[7]). The note's wording 「惲弟俁，俁弟詵，詵弟顗」[3] gives the sequence Yun → Yu → Shen → Yi, and 「顗弟粲」[6] places Can after Yi; so I infer Can was the youngest, though the text does not explicitly say "youngest son."
- Xun Yun's sons Xun Han 荀甝 and Xun Ji 荀霬, and Xun Yu's grandson Xun Yu 荀寓 [17], are the next generation, not Xun Yu's sons. Note also a *different* Xun Yun (courtesy name Jingwen 景文) appears in the Pei notes [2] — a cousin, not to be confused with Xun Yu's son.

以下不是《三国志》的记载: The question asks about "offices each of them held," but for Xun Can the *Sanguozhi* records no office at all; later sources outside this record (such as accounts of the Xun clan) sometimes supply one, but that is not part of the *Sanguozhi* text.

q: How many different people named Ma Zhong appear in the Records of the Three Kingdoms?
reply:
**答案：《三国志》里出现了两位不同的“马忠”。** 一位是蜀汉的将领马忠（字德信），一位是东吴潘璋部下的司马马忠。

---

### 一、蜀汉的马忠，字德信

他的本传在《蜀书十三》（黄李吕马王张传）。他原本姓狐名笃，后来恢复本姓改名忠：

「馬忠字德信，巴西閬中人也。少養外家，姓狐，名篤，後乃復姓，改名忠。」[1]

先主刘备在猇亭战败后见到他，对尚书令刘巴说：「雖亡黃權，復得狐篤，此為世不乏賢也。」[1]

他历仕诸葛亮、蒋琬时期，做到庲降都督、镇南大将军，封彭乡亭侯，延熙十二年去世：

「延熙五年還朝……加拜鎮南大將軍。……十二年卒，子脩嗣。」[2]

裴注还补记了他的后人：「脩弟恢。恢子義，晉建寧太守。」[3]

### 二、东吴的马忠，潘璋的司马

这位马忠没有自己的传，只在孙权征关羽时出现。建安二十四年（据《吴主传》正文所记年月）十二月：

「權先使朱然、潘璋斷其徑路。十二月，璋司馬馬忠獲羽及其子平、都督趙累等於章鄉，遂定荊州。」[6]

《潘璋传》也记同一件事：「權征關羽，璋與朱然斷羽走道，到臨沮，住夾石。璋部下司馬馬忠禽羽，并羽子平、都督趙累等。」[10]

据此可知，这位马忠是潘璋部下的司马，因擒获关羽父子而留名。

---

**小结：** 一位是蜀汉名将马忠（德信），一位是东吴潘璋的司马马忠，两人同名，时代相近，但分属两国、身份地位悬殊，是《三国志》中容易混淆的同名人物。

q: Which emperor was stabbed to death in the street?
reply:
The emperor was **Cao Mao (曹髦), the Duke of Gaogui Township (高貴鄉公)**, killed in 260 CE.

## Who he was

Cao Mao was a grandson of Emperor Wen (曹丕) through the Prince of Donghai, Cao Lin (曹霖). The Empress Dowager's order states: 「東海王霖，高祖文皇帝之子。霖之諸子，與國至親，高貴鄉公髦有大成之量，其以為明皇帝嗣。」 [15] — i.e., he was made heir to Emperor Ming (明帝).

## The killing

According to the main text of the *Wei Records* (魏書), in the fifth year of Ganlu (甘露五年), on the day *ji-chou* of the fifth month: 「五月己丑，高貴鄉公卒，年二十。」 [17] The official report by the Grand General Sima Wen-wang (司馬文王, i.e., Sima Zhao) says: 「騎督成倅弟太子舍人濟，橫入兵陣傷公，遂至隕命；輙收濟行軍法。」 [12] — Cheng Ji (成濟), a Retainer of the Heir Apparent and younger brother of the Cavalry Commandant Cheng Cui, thrust into the ranks and wounded him, causing his death.

The circumstances are recorded in Pei Songzhi's annotations. Pei notes that Xi Zuochi's *Han-Jin Chunqiu* (漢晉春秋) is the most orderly account, so he places it first [11]:

> 「帝遂帥僮僕數百，鼓譟而出。文王弟屯騎校尉伷入，遇帝於東止車門，左右呵之，伷衆奔走。中護軍賈充又逆帝戰於南闕下，帝自用劒。衆欲退，太子舍人成濟問充曰：『事急矣。當云何？』充曰：『畜養汝等，正謂今日。今日之事，無所問也。』濟即前刺帝，刃出於背。」 [11]

So Cao Mao rode out with several hundred servants, shouting and beating drums; he fought personally with his sword at the south gate tower, and it was **Cheng Ji, at Jia Chong's (賈充) urging, who ran him through from behind**, the blade coming out his back. Sima Zhao, hearing of it, threw himself to the ground and said: 「天下其謂我何！」 [11]

Pei Songzhi records several differing accounts of the same event:
- Gan Bao's *Jin Ji* (干寶《晉紀》): Cheng Ji asked Jia Chong, and Chong answered, 「公畜養汝等，為今日之事也。夫何疑！」 whereupon 「濟曰：『然。』乃抽戈犯蹕。」 [14]
- *Wei Mo Zhuan* (《魏末傳》): Jia Chong called out to Cheng Ji, 「司馬家事若敗，汝等豈復有種乎？何不出擊！」 and to the question 「當殺邪？執邪？」 Chong replied, 「殺之。」 「濟兄弟因前刺帝，帝倒車下。」 [13]
- *Wei Shi Chunqiu* (《魏氏春秋》): 「騎督成倅弟成濟以矛進，帝崩于師。時暴雨雷霆，晦冥。」 [14]

Note the variation in weapon and wording: 刺 (stabbed) in the first two, 以矛進 (advanced with a spear) in the third.

## Aftermath

The Grand General then had Cheng Ji executed, but Pei's *Wei Shi Chunqiu* says he did not submit quietly: 「成濟兄弟不即伏罪，袒而升屋，醜言悖慢；自下射之，乃殪。」 [16] The Empress Dowager's edict placed the blame on Cao Mao's own conduct [17].

## Date

The *era* tool converts Ganlu 5 (甘露五年) to **260 CE**. The main text records the death in the fifth month (五月己丑) [17].

---

The episode is often remembered for Cao Mao's line, recorded in the *Han-Jin Chunqiu*: 「司馬昭之心，路人所知也。吾不能坐受廢辱，今日當與卿等自出討之。」 [11]

q: Who were the sons of Emperor Zhaolie?
reply:
**Conclusion:** "Emperor Zhaolie" (昭烈皇帝) is the posthumous title of Liu Bei, the founding emperor of Shu Han (reigned from Zhangwu 1 = AD 221). The *Records of the Three Kingdoms* records three biological sons and one adopted son:

- **Liu Shan (劉禪)**, styled Gongsi (公嗣), the heir — declared Crown Prince (皇太子)
- **Liu Yong (劉永)**, styled Gongshou (公壽)
- **Liu Li (劉理)**, styled Fengxiao (奉孝)
- **Liu Feng (劉封)** — an **adopted** son (養子), not a biological one

**Evidence**

In Zhangwu 1 (AD 221), when Liu Bei took the imperial title, he enfeoffed his sons:

「章武元年夏四月，大赦，改年……五月，立皇后吳氏，子禪為皇太子。六月，以子永為魯王，理為梁王。」[14]

Liu Shan's own biography confirms he was Liu Bei's son and heir:

「後主諱禪，字公嗣，先主子也。建安二十四年，先主為漢中王，立為王太子。」[2]

The *Biographies of the Two Sovereigns' Consorts and Sons* separately records Liu Yong and Liu Li, both called Liu Shan's younger half-brothers:

「劉永字公壽，先主子，後主庶弟也。章武元年六月，使司徒靖立永為魯王……建興八年，改封為甘陵王。」[13]

「劉理字奉孝，亦後主庶弟也，與永異母。章武元年六月，使司徒靖立理為梁王……建興八年，改封理為安平王。」[12]

Note that these two were brothers of Liu Shan by different mothers from each other (「與永異母」[12]).

The adopted son:

「劉封者，本羅侯寇氏之子，長沙劉氏之甥也。先主至荊州，以未有繼嗣，養封為子。」[18]

So Liu Feng was originally a son of the Kou family of Luohou, taken in by Liu Bei when Liu Bei had no heir yet. He was later forced to commit suicide on Liu Bei's and Zhuge Liang's order [23].

**Inference (推斷):** Since Liu Yong and Liu Li are both called Liu Shan's "younger half-brothers" (庶弟) and were enfeoffed only in Zhangwu 1, while Liu Shan had already been made King's Heir in Jian'an 24 (AD 219) and Crown Prince in Zhangwu 1, it follows that Liu Shan was the eldest of Liu Bei's sons by a principal wife's status, and Yong and Li were junior sons. This is inference from the enfeoffment order and the wording, not an explicit statement of birth order.

**Note:** Liu Bei's own posthumous title "Zhaolie" (昭烈) is not what the *Sanguozhi* main text uses for him — the text consistently calls him 「先主」 ("the Former Lord"). The title "昭烈皇帝" is his temple/posthumous designation, and the term "Emperor Zhaolie" is not itself a *Sanguozhi* wording.

q: How many emperors did the state of Wu have?
reply:
## How many emperors did Wu have?

**Four men actually reigned as emperor of Wu** — Sun Quan, Sun Liang, Sun Xiu, and Sun Hao. In addition, **two men who never reigned were posthumously given imperial titles** — Sun Jian and Sun He. So the count depends on whether you mean "rulers who took the throne" (4) or "people who held the imperial title" (6).

### The four reigning emperors

**Sun Quan** (the founder) — 「丙申，南郊即皇帝位。是日大赦。改年，追尊父破虜將軍堅爲武烈皇帝，母吳氏爲武烈皇后，兄討逆將軍策爲長沙桓王」[1] ("On the bing-shen day he ascended the imperial throne at the southern suburb... he changed the era name, and posthumously honored his father, the General Who Breaks the Enemy Sun Jian, as Emperor Wulie").

**Sun Liang** (son of Sun Quan) — 「明年四月，權薨，太子即尊號，大赦，改」[11] ("The next year in the fourth month, Sun Quan died; the heir ascended the honored title, granted a general amnesty, and changed the era"). He was later deposed: 「黜亮爲會稽王，時年十六」[16] ("They deposed Sun Liang as Prince of Kuaiji; he was sixteen at the time").

**Sun Xiu** (sixth son of Sun Quan) — after Sun Liang was deposed, Sun Chen's men welcomed him: 「孫綝使宗正孫楷與中書郎董朝迎休...即日，御正殿，大赦，改元」[30] ("Sun Chen sent the Imperial Clan Officer Sun Kai and the Secretariat Gentleman Dong Chao to welcome Sun Xiu... that same day he took the main hall, granted a general amnesty, and changed the era").

**Sun Hao** (grandson of Sun Quan, son of Sun He) — 「於是遂迎立皓，時年二十三。改元，大赦」[29] ("So they then welcomed and enthroned Sun Hao; he was twenty-three at the time. He changed the era and granted a general amnesty"). He was the last ruler, surrendering to Jin: 「壬申，王濬最先到，於是受皓之降」[34] ("On the ren-shen day, Wang Jun arrived first and thereupon received Sun Hao's surrender").

The official histories group the last three together as the "Biographies of the Three Successor Rulers" (三嗣主傳) [48].

### The two posthumously honored emperors

**Sun Jian** (Sun Quan's father) — honored by Sun Quan: 「追尊父破虜將軍堅爲武烈皇帝」[1], and again noted at [4]: 「權旣稱尊號，諡堅曰武烈皇帝」 ("When Sun Quan took the honored title, he gave Sun Jian the posthumous name Emperor Wulie").

**Sun He** (Sun Hao's father) — honored by Sun Hao: 「皓即位，尊和為昭獻皇帝」[19] ("When Sun Hao took the throne, he honored Sun He as Emperor Zhaoxian"). Pei Songzhi's note quoting the *Wu Lu* adds: 「皓初尊和為昭獻皇帝，俄改曰文皇帝」[31] ("Sun Hao first honored Sun He as Emperor Zhaoxian, and soon after changed it to Emperor Wen").

### Basis for the count (inference)

The records list exactly four men who "ascended the honored title" or "ascended the throne" in Wu — Sun Quan [1], Sun Liang [11], Sun Xiu [30], and Sun Hao [29]. Two further men received imperial posthumous names from those rulers but are never recorded as reigning: Sun Jian [1][4] and Sun He [19][31]. From this it follows that Wu had four actual emperors, with two additional posthumous imperial honorees. Note that Sun Quan's brother Sun Ce was honored only as Prince Huan of Changsha (長沙桓王), not as emperor [1].

q: Why did Cao Cao flee from Luoyang?
reply:
## Conclusion

According to the *Sanguozhi*, Cao Cao fled Luoyang because Dong Zhuo, who had just seized control of the capital by deposing the emperor and installing Emperor Xian, offered Cao Cao an appointment in order to keep him as an advisor — and Cao Cao refused it, changed his name, and slipped away eastward.

## The record

The main text of the *Wudi ji* (Annals of Emperor Wu) says:

> 「卓到，廢帝爲弘農王而立獻帝，京都大亂。卓表太祖爲驍騎校尉，欲與計事。太祖乃變易姓名，間行東歸。」[6]

Translation: Dong Zhuo arrived, deposed the emperor as Prince of Hongnong and set up Emperor Xian, and the capital fell into great disorder. Dong Zhuo memorialized to appoint the Grand Ancestor (Cao Cao) as Colonel of the Agile Cavalry, wishing to consult with him on affairs. The Grand Ancestor then changed his name and traveled by side roads eastward home.

So the sequence given is: Dong Zhuo's takeover of Luoyang → Dong Zhuo's offer of the post of Xiaoqi Xiaowei (Colonel of the Agile Cavalry), intending to use Cao Cao → Cao Cao's refusal, flight, and change of name. This took place in 中平六年 = 189 CE [era tool], the year the main text explicitly fixes for the end of this passage: 「是歲中平六年也」[6].

The Pei Songzhi annotation fills in Cao Cao's motive more directly. Pei注引《魏書》:

> 「太祖以卓終必覆敗，遂不就拜，逃歸鄉里。」[12]

Translation: The Grand Ancestor, judging that Dong Zhuo would in the end certainly be overthrown and defeated, did not accept the appointment and fled back to his home district.

So the *Wei Shu* explanation is that Cao Cao refused the post and fled precisely because he concluded Dong Zhuo was doomed.

## The flight itself

The main text continues: on the way out of the pass, at Zhongmu, Cao Cao was suspected by the local constable and taken to the county office, but someone there recognized him and interceded, so he was released [6]. 裴注引《世語》 adds that the county clerk knew who he was and argued that in a time of disorder one should not detain a hero, and so reported to the magistrate to free him [19]. He then reached Chenliu, dispersed his family wealth, gathered righteous troops, and in the twelfth month raised his army at Jiwu, intending to attack Dong Zhuo [6]. 裴注引《世語》 says the Chenliu filial and incorrupt Wei Zi funded him with his family fortune, giving him a force of five thousand [20].

The famous Lü Boshe episode belongs here as well, and Pei Songzhi records several versions: 裴注引《魏書》 says Lü Boshe was absent and his son and guests seized Cao Cao for his horse and goods, and Cao Cao killed several of them with his own hand; 《世語》 says Cao Cao, having defied Dong Zhuo's order, suspected them of plotting against him and killed eight people at night; and Sun Sheng's *Zaji* says he heard the sound of food vessels and thought they meant to harm him, killed them at night, then said 「寧我負人，毋人負我！」[12]. These accounts differ, and I am not adjudicating between them — I simply note them side by side.

## Points of inference (marked as inference)

Drawing only on the facts cited above: (1) Dong Zhuo had "specialized in deposing and setting up" emperors and held the arsenal and state treasures, "overawing the world," and was "cruel and unmerciful," punishing the slightest grudge so that "no one could keep himself safe" [14]; (2) Dong Zhuo wanted Cao Cao as an advisor and gave him a military post [6]; (3) Cao Cao judged that Dong Zhuo would fail and refused [12]. From these, one may infer that Cao Cao's flight was both a refusal to serve the new regime and a personal escape: refusing the post meant defying a man who, on the record just quoted, killed even for trifling grudges — hence the changed name and side roads [6]. The records do not state that fear of Dong Zhuo's cruelty was his motive; that is inference, whereas the *Wei Shu* motive stated in the text is his judgment that Dong Zhuo would be defeated [12].

## Background

q: Where did Taishi Ci and Sun Ce fight each other? Later, when Taishi Ci was captured, how did Sun Ce treat him?
reply:
**Conclusion: The two first fought at Shenting (神亭), and Taishi Ci was later captured at Jingxian (涇縣). When captured, Sun Ce personally untied him, took his hand, and put him to use as his own officer.**

## The first encounter — at Shenting

The main biography records that Taishi Ci was then serving Yangzhou Inspector Liu Yao, who sent him only to scout out Sun Ce's strength:

「但使慈偵視輕重。時獨與一騎卒遇策。策從騎十三，皆韓當、宋謙、黃蓋輩也。慈便前鬥，正與策對。策刺慈馬，而攬得慈項上手戟，慈亦得策兜鍪。會兩家兵騎並各來赴，於是解散。」[1]

Taishi Ci met Sun Ce while out scouting; Sun Ce had thirteen riders (Han Dang, Song Qian, Huang Gai and others). Sun Ce stabbed Taishi Ci's horse and seized the hand-halberd at his neck; Taishi Ci in turn got Sun Ce's helmet; both sides' troops arrived and they broke off.

The place is named 神亭 (Shenting) — Sun Ce himself recalls it later: 「寧識神亭時邪？」[6], and the Pei Songzhi commentary quotes the *Wu Li*: 「慈於神亭戰敗，為策所執。」[2]

## The capture — at Jingxian

After Liu Yao's defeat, Taishi Ci fled to Wuhu, hid in the mountains, and styled himself Danyang Administrator. He then advanced to Jingxian, set up a camp, and gathered many Shanyue:

「慈因進住涇縣，立屯府，大為山越所附。策躬自攻討，遂見囚執。」[6]

Sun Ce attacked him in person, and Taishi Ci was taken prisoner.

## How Sun Ce treated him

「策即解縛，捉其手曰：『寧識神亭時邪？若卿爾時得我云何？』慈曰：『未可量也。』策大笑曰：『今日之事，當與卿共之。』即署門下督，還吳授兵，拜折衝中郎將。」[6]

Sun Ce at once untied him, took his hand, jested about Shenting ("If you had caught me then, what would you have done?" — "Hard to say"), laughed, and said the present enterprise should be shared with him. He appointed Taishi Ci Menxia Du (门下督), gave him troops on return to Wu, and made him Chongzhong General of the Household Gentlemen (折衝中郎將).

Sun Ce also entrusted him with a delicate mission — to reassure the followers of the late Liu Yao and to scout out Hua Xin (子魚)'s situation — over his officers' objections, saying: 「子義捨我，當復與誰？」[6] Taishi Ci returned on schedule. The *Jiang Biao Zhuan* adds Sun Ce's defense of him: 「太史子義雖氣勇有膽烈，然非縱橫之人……一以意許知己，死亡不相負，諸君勿復憂也。」[5]

## A discrepancy in the sources

The main biography places the capture at Jingxian, after a separate fight. The *Wu Li*, quoted in Pei's commentary, instead says Taishi Ci was captured when defeated at Shenting itself: 「慈於神亭戰敗，為策所執。」[2] Pei Songzhi does not accept this: 「臣松之案：吳歷云慈於神亭戰敗，為策所得，與本傳大異，疑為謬誤。」[2] The two accounts are given side by side; the *Wu Li* version also supplies the detail of Sun Ce's long-kneeling answer and his waiting at noon with a pole to measure the shadow for Taishi Ci's promised return [2].

---

以下不是《三国志》的记载:

In the novel *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, the Shenting duel between Taishi Ci and Sun Ce is elaborated into an extended single combat, but the basic facts (the fight at Shenting and the later capture) do come from the historical record as shown above.

Shenting (神亭) was in the area of present-day Danyang/Jintan, Jiangsu.

q: How did Chang Ho die?
reply:
**Conclusion**

Zhang He (張郃, courtesy name Junchi 雋乂) was killed by an arrow while pursuing Zhuge Liang's retreating army, in 231 (the 9th year of Zhuge Liang's Jianxing era). He was posthumously given the title Marquis Zhuang (壯侯), and his son Zhang Xiong (張雄) inherited his rank.

**What the sources say**

Chen Shou's own text in Zhang He's biography:

- 「諸葛亮復出祁山，詔郃督諸將西至略陽，亮還保祁山，郃追至木門，與亮軍交戰，飛矢中郃右膝，薨，諡曰壯侯。子雄嗣。」[2] — Zhuge Liang came out of Qishan again; Zhang He was ordered west to Lüeyang; when Zhuge Liang fell back to hold Qishan, Zhang He pursued him to Mumen, fought Zhuge Liang's army, and a flying arrow struck his right knee; he died, and was given the posthumous name Marquis Zhuang. His son Zhang Xiong succeeded him.

The date is given in the Later Ruler's annals (Shu 3), which places it in the same campaign:

- 「九年春二月，亮復出軍圍祁山，始以木牛運。魏司馬懿、張郃救祁山。夏六月，亮糧盡退軍，郃追至青封，與亮交戰，被箭死。」[7] — In the 2nd month of the 9th year [of Jianxing], Zhuge Liang again sent out troops and besieged Qishan… In the 6th month, Zhuge Liang's provisions ran out and he withdrew; Zhang He pursued to Qingfeng, fought Zhuge Liang, and died of an arrow wound.

The 9th year of Jianxing = 231 AD [era tool].

Zhuge Liang's own biography gives the same outcome: 「九年，亮復出祁山，以木牛運，糧盡退軍，與魏將張郃交戰，射殺郃。」[15]

**Pei Songzhi's supplementary note (裴注引《魏略》)**

Pei's note to the biography quotes the Weilüe, which adds detail and puts the blame on Sima Yi:

- 裴注引《魏略》: 「亮軍退，司馬宣王使郃追之，郃曰：『軍法，圍城必開出路，歸軍勿追。』宣王不聽。郃不得已，遂進。蜀軍乘高布伏，弓弩亂發，矢中郃髀。」[13] — When Zhuge Liang's army withdrew, Sima Xuanwang (Sima Yi) made Zhang He pursue. Zhang He said, "By military law, a besieged city must be left a way out, and a retreating army must not be pursued." Xuanwang did not listen. Zhang He had no choice but to advance. The Shu army took the high ground and set an ambush; bows and crossbows fired in volleys, and an arrow struck Zhang He's thigh.

Another note, quoting the Weilüe in the Xin Pi biography, says simply: 「諸葛亮圍祁山，不克，引退。張郃追之，爲流矢所中死。」[4] — Zhuge Liang besieged Qishan, failed to take it, and withdrew; Zhang He pursued him and died from a stray arrow.

**Inference**

Putting these together, it may be inferred (據此推斷) that Zhang He died of an arrow wound received while chasing Zhuge Liang's withdrawing army after the Qishan campaign of 231: the Later Ruler's annals gives the month (6th month of the 9th year) and the place name Qingfeng [7], while Zhang He's biography gives Mumen [2], and the Weilüe adds that Sima Yi ordered the pursuit over Zhang He's objection [13].

Note that the sources disagree on details, and these should be considered separately rather than resolved:
- The place of the pursuit: 木門 in Zhang He's biography [2] vs. 青封 in the Later Ruler's annals [7].
- The wound: 右膝 ("right knee") in Chen Shou's text [2] vs. 髀 ("thigh") in the Weilüe [13].
- Whether Sima Yi compelled the pursuit: the Weilüe says he did and that Zhang He objected [13]; Chen Shou's text records only that Zhang He pursued [2]. Pei Songzhi, in the note at Xin Pi's biography, remarks that the Weilüe "本來就已經難以相信" (is already hard to trust) [4].

**Background**

以下不是《三国志》的记载:

The best-known version of Zhang He's death — that Sima Yi deliberately sent him to his death out of jealousy or as a factional move — is a later elaboration; the Weilüe account [13] has Sima Yi ordering the pursuit against Zhang He's advice, but it says nothing about ill intent, and Pei Songzhi himself doubts the Weilüe's reliability. The dramatic form of this story in popular tradition comes from non-orthodox sources rather than Chen Shou's text.

Mumen (木門) and Qingfeng (青封), the places named for the pursuit, are in the present-day Gansu/Shaanxi border region of the old Longxi–Hanzhong route.

q: At Hefei, facing Sun Quan's army of a hundred thousand, how many picked men did Zhang Liao lead in his charge?
reply:
**结论：八百人。**

据《三国志·魏书·张辽传》，曹操征张鲁时留给护军薛悌一道教令，孙权率十万众围合肥时拆开，教令命张辽、李典出战。张辽当夜募勇士：

「於是遼夜募敢從之士，得八百人，椎牛饗將士，明日大戰。」[1]

第二天天亮，张辽「被甲持戟，先登陷陳，殺數十人，斬二將，大呼自名，衝壘入，至權麾下」[1]，一直冲到孙权的麾旗之下，孙权惊走登高冢。后来张辽突围而出，听见余众呼喊「將軍棄我乎」，又回身杀入重围把他们救出，「自旦戰至日中，吳人奪氣」[1]。

后来魏文帝追念此功，诏书中也说得很明确：

「合肥之役，遼典以步卒八百，破賊十萬，自古用兵，未之有也。」[7]

所以冲击孙权十万大军的，是张辽（与李典一同）率领的八百名应募步卒。

以下不是《三国志》的记载：
- 《三国演义》里常说张辽"威震逍遥津"、以八百破十万，正史所载的数目（八百破十万）与演义一致；不过正史中迎击的教令是命张辽、李典出战、乐进守城，并非张辽一人独断 [1][2]。

q: When Zhuge Liang lit the seven-star lamps at Wuzhang Plains to prolong his life, who burst in and put them out?
reply:
## Short answer

The seven-star lamp ritual (七星灯／祈禳) at Wuzhang Plains, and the man who rushes in and puts the lamps out, are **not in the *Sanguozhi*** (《三国志》) at all. That whole episode is a creation of *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* (《三国演义》), where the intruder is **Wei Yan (魏延)**. Chen Shou's history records only that Zhuge Liang fell ill and died at Wuzhang Plains; it says nothing about lamps, prayers for long life, or anyone bursting into the tent and extinguishing them.

## What the *Sanguozhi* actually records

The *Zhuge Liang Zhuan* (蜀书·诸葛亮传) gives only this for his death at Wuzhang Plains:

> 「十二年春，亮悉大眾由斜谷出，以流馬運，據武功五丈原，與司馬宣王對於渭南……相持百餘日。其年八月，亮疾病，卒于軍，時年五十四。」[1]

(In the 12th year of Jianxing, spring, Zhuge Liang led his whole army out through Xie Valley, used "wooden flowing horses" for transport, occupied Wuzhang Plains in Wugong, and faced Sima Xuanwang south of the Wei River… They stood off for over a hundred days. In the eighth month of that year, Zhuge Liang fell ill and died in the army, aged fifty-four.)

The *Houzhu Zhuan* (蜀书·后主传) agrees, and even here there is no lamp ritual — the only event attached to his death is the quarrel between Wei Yan and Yang Yi:

> 「十二年春二月，亮由斜谷出，始以流馬運。秋八月，亮卒渭濱。征西大將軍魏延與丞相長史楊儀爭權不和，舉兵相攻，延敗走。」[7]

(In the 12th year, spring, second month, Liang went out through Xie Valley… Autumn, eighth month, Liang died on the bank of the Wei River. The General of the Western Conquest Wei Yan and the Chief Clerk of the Chancellor Yang Yi quarreled over power and attacked each other; Yan was defeated and fled.)

What the sources do describe is Zhuge Liang's illness and Sima Yi's assessment of it — again with no lamps:

> 裴注引《魏氏春秋》:「諸葛公夙興夜寐，罰二十以上，皆親攬焉；所啖食不至數升。」宣王曰：「亮將死矣。」[11]

(Pei Songzhi's commentary quoting the *Wei shi chunqiu*: "The Duke of Zhuge rises early and sleeps late; for any punishment of twenty strokes or more he attends to it himself; what he eats is less than a few pints." Xuanwang said: "Liang is about to die.")

> 裴注引《晉陽秋》:「有星赤而芒角，自東北西南流，投于亮營，三投再還，往大還小。俄而亮卒。」[2]

(Pei Songzhi's commentary quoting the *Jin yangqiu*: "There was a star, red and with rays, that flowed from northeast to southwest and fell into Liang's camp, falling three times and returning twice, going out large and coming back small. Soon afterward Liang died.")

Note that this last item is a *star* omen in the sky over the camp, not lamps in the tent lit to extend his life; and it comes from the *Jin yangqiu*, not from Chen Shou's main text.

## Basis for the conclusion (inference)

From the facts above: (1) the *Sanguozhi* main text records Zhuge Liang's death at Wuzhang Plains in the eighth month of Jianxing 12 with no ritual of any kind [1][7]; (2) the only "extra" material in Pei Songzhi's notes about his final days concerns his overwork and eating little [11], and an omen of a falling star [2]; (3) nothing anywhere describes seven lamps, prayers for longevity, or a tent intruder. Therefore the lamp episode cannot be drawn from the *Sanguozhi*; it must come from a different tradition — specifically the novel. This is an inference from the sources, not a claim that the event "did not happen," since absence of record is not proof.

## Background

The following is not a record from the *Sanguozhi*: the story that Zhuge Liang lit seven-star lamps at Wuzhang Plains to pray for an extension of his life, and that Wei Yan burst into the tent and extinguished the lamps, has no record in the *Sanguozhi* and comes from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* or other non-official accounts.

q: During his southern campaign, how many times did Zhuge Liang capture and release Meng Huo?
reply:
**Short answer: seven times.** According to the source, Zhuge Liang released Meng Huo and captured him again on seven separate occasions — the phrase used is "seven releases, seven captures."

**Evidence**

The account comes not from Chen Shou's main text of the *Zhuge Liang* biography, but from Pei Songzhi's annotation, which quotes the *Han–Jin Spring and Autumn Annals* (《漢晉春秋》):

「亮笑，縱使更戰，七縱七禽，而亮猶遣獲。獲止不去，曰：『公，天威也，南人不復反矣。』」[1]

— "Zhuge Liang laughed, released him to fight again; seven times he released and seven times he captured him, and Zhuge Liang still meant to send Meng Huo away. Meng Huo stopped and would not leave, saying: 'Sir, this is Heaven's majesty; the southerners will not rebel again.'"

The same annotation goes on to say that after reaching Dianchi (滇池) and pacifying the south, Zhuge Liang employed the local chieftains themselves to govern [1].

A related note in the *Ma Liang* biography, quoting the *Xiangyang Record* (《襄陽記》), records Ma Su's advice to Zhuge Liang on this campaign — "attack the heart above all, attack the walls below" (「攻心為上，攻城為下」) — and says Zhuge Liang "adopted his plan, pardoned Meng Huo to win over the south, and therefore throughout Zhuge Liang's lifetime the south did not dare rebel again" (「亮納其策，赦孟獲以服南方。故終亮之世，南方不敢復反」) [2].

**Source note:** The "seven captures and seven releases" figure rests on Pei Songzhi's annotation quoting 《漢晉春秋》 [1]. Chen Shou's own text of the biography does not relate this episode; the standard *Sanguozhi* narrative simply records that Zhuge Liang campaigned in the south and pacified it.

q: How did Cao Cao view Liu Bei when Liu Bei came over to his side?
reply:
## Conclusion

When Liu Bei came over to Cao Cao's side, Cao Cao treated him with conspicuous honor and generosity, publicly rating him as a true "hero" (英雄) on a par with himself — yet he also recognized that Liu Bei was a man of "heroic talent" who would never stay under another man, and he twice refused advice to kill him, judging that the political cost of destroying a talented man who had sought refuge with him would be worse than the danger. So his view was a mix of admiration/desire to use him, and underlying wariness — which in the end proved justified when Liu Bei turned against him.

## What the records say

**1. The circumstances of Liu Bei's arrival.** Liu Bei first came to Cao Cao after being beaten by Lü Bu:
「呂布惡之，自出兵攻先主，先主敗走歸曹公。曹公厚遇之，以為豫州牧。」[37] ("Lü Bu resented him, sent out troops himself to attack the Former Lord; the Former Lord was defeated and fled to join Lord Cao. Lord Cao treated him generously and made him Governor of Yuzhou.")

**2. How he was received — high honors and closeness.**
「先主復得妻子，從曹公還許。表先主為左將軍，禮之愈重，出則同輿，坐則同席。」[37] ("The Former Lord got his wife and children back again, and followed Lord Cao back to Xu. He memorialized to make the Former Lord General of the Left, and treated him with ever greater ceremony: when going out they rode in the same carriage, when sitting they shared the same mat.")

**3. Cao Cao's own judgment — the "hero" remark.** In the Xu capital:
「是時曹公從容謂先主曰：『今天下英雄，唯使君與操耳。本初之徒，不足數也。』」[6] ("At that time Lord Cao calmly said to the Former Lord: 'The heroes of the world today are only you, my lord, and me — Cao. The likes of Yuan Benchu are not worth counting.'") The Former Lord was so startled he dropped his spoon and chopsticks [6]; Pei Songzhi's note adds that there happened to be a thunderclap and Liu Bei used it as an excuse [22].

**4. Cao Cao rejected advice to kill him — twice.**
- Cheng Yu: 「程昱說公曰：『觀劉備有雄才而甚得衆心，終不爲人下，不如早圖之。』公曰：『方今收英雄時也，殺一人而失天下之心，不可。』」[9] ("Cheng Yu persuaded Lord Cao: 'Looking at Liu Bei, he has heroic talent and greatly wins men's hearts; he will never be another's subordinate — better to deal with him early.' Lord Cao said: 'Now is the time for gathering heroes; to kill one man and lose the hearts of the world — that cannot be done.'")
- Guo Jia (per Pei Songzhi's citations): 「《魏書》曰：劉備來奔，以為豫州牧。或謂太祖曰：『備有英雄志，今不早圖，後必為患。』太祖以問嘉，嘉曰：『……今備有英雄名，以窮歸己而害之，是以害賢為名，則智士將自疑，回心擇主，公誰與定天下？夫除一人之患，以沮四海之望，安危之機，不可不察！』太祖笑曰：『君得之矣。』」[4] ("The Wei Shu says: Liu Bei came to flee to him, and he made him Governor of Yuzhou. Someone said to the Grand Progenitor: 'Bei has heroic ambitions; if you do not plan against him early, he will surely be a later trouble.' The Grand Progenitor asked Guo Jia, and Jia said: '...Now Bei has a hero's name; to harm him because he has come to you in extremity is to gain the name of harming the worthy — then wise men will doubt you, turn their hearts and choose another lord. With whom will you settle the world? To remove one man's threat while dashing the hopes of the four seas — this is the pivot of safety and danger, which must be examined!' The Grand Progenitor laughed and said: 'You have got it.'")
- Pei Songzhi also cites the Fu Zi that Guo Jia separately warned Cao Cao: 「備有雄才而甚得眾心。張飛、關羽者，皆萬人之敵也，為之死用。嘉觀之，備終不為人下，其謀未可測也……宜早為之所。」and that at this time Cao Cao 「方招懷英雄以明大信，未得從嘉謀」[4] ("was just then winning over heroes to display great good faith, and did not follow Guo Jia's plan").

**5. Cao Cao's later verdict — a real threat.** After Liu Bei's defection and revolt, Cao Cao said: 「夫劉備，人傑也，今不擊，必爲後患。」[12] ("Liu Bei is an outstanding man; if we do not strike now, he will surely be a later trouble.") Sun Sheng's Wei Shi Chunqiu likewise has him telling his generals: 「劉備，人傑也，將生憂寡人。」[3] ("Liu Bei is an outstanding man; he will cause me grief.") Pei Songzhi, however, cautions that historians embellish recorded speeches and he finds this particular wording questionable [3].

## My inference (based on the facts above)

Drawing only on the above: (a) Cao Cao gave Liu Bei the offices of Yuzhou Governor and then General of the Left, and the privileges of shared carriage and mat [37]; (b) he called him the one man in the world worthy to be ranked with himself [6]; (c) he declined Cheng Yu's and Guo Jia's suggestions to kill him, on the stated ground that it would cost him the allegiance of talented men [9][4]; (d) at the same time both advisers warned that Liu Bei would never be anyone's subordinate, and Cao Cao accepted that assessment ("You have got it") [4]; and (e) once Liu Bei had actually turned against him, Cao Cao called him an outstanding man and a future menace that had to be struck [12][3]. From these I infer that Cao Cao's view was double-sided: he genuinely rated Liu Bei highly and wanted to keep and use him, and he deliberately refrained from killing him for reasons of reputation and political recruitment — not because he thought him harmless. The fact that he spoke of Liu Bei as an equal (hero) at one moment and as a threat to be struck down at the next shows the high regard and the wariness coexisted.

## Note on sources

The "煮酒论英雄" scene and the thunderclap episode appear here in the Sanguozhi and its Pei notes [6][22] in compressed form; the fuller dramatic staging (the garden, the enumeration of rival lords, etc.) is the Sanguo Yanyi version. The record gives no specific calendar date attached to Liu Bei's first coming-over itself; the Fu Zi says only 「初，劉備來降」[4], and the Hero Ji dates Lü Bu's breaking of Liu Bei's Pei city to the ninth month of Jian'an 3 (198 CE) [20], with Liu Bei meeting Cao Cao in Liang territory in the tenth month [20].

以下不是《三国志》的记载: The scene of "煮酒论英雄" as popularly told — the two men in a garden drinking wine while Liu Bei nervously enumerates the great lords and is then startled by thunder — is the Sanguo Yanyi version; the Sanguozhi itself records only Cao Cao's "hero" remark and Liu Bei's dropping his utensils, with Pei's note supplying the thunderclap [6][22].

q: In which year did Sima Yi remove Cao Shuang from power and take control of the government?
reply:
**Answer: 249 AD (the first year of the Jiaping 嘉平 era, in the first month).**

This is the event known as the Gaopingling 高平陵 incident. The record in the *Sanguozhi* says:

- In the *Wei Shu, Annals of the Three Young Emperors (Duke of Qi)*: 「嘉平元年春正月甲午，車駕謁高平陵。太傅司馬宣王奏免大將軍曹爽、爽弟中領軍羲、武衞將軍訓、散騎常侍彥官，以侯就第。」[1] — In the spring, first month of the first year of Jiaping, the imperial carriage went to pay respects at Gaopingling. The Grand Tutor Sima Xuanwang (Sima Yi) submitted a memorial removing from office the Grand General Cao Shuang, his brothers the Central Army Commander Cao Xi, the Wuwei General Cao Xun, and the Cavalier Attendant Regular Cao Yan, sending them home as marquises.

The same block records the aftermath: 「戊戌，有司奏収黃門張當付廷尉，考實其辭，爽與謀不軌。……皆與爽通姦謀，夷三族。」[1] — the officials had the Yellow Gate Zhang Dang arrested and interrogated, and Cao Shuang, along with Ding Mi, Deng Yang, He Yan, Bi Gui, Li Sheng and Huan Fan, were all executed with extinction of their three clans.

The *Wei Shu, Xiahou and Cao biographies* give the background of the struggle: Cao Shuang, after Emperor Ming's death, was one of the two regents alongside Sima Yi, but he had Sima Yi transferred to Grand Tutor and pushed him out of actual power: 「丁謐畫策，使爽白天子，發詔轉宣王爲太傅，外以名號尊之，內欲令尚書奏事，先來由己，得制其輕重也」[2]; and Sima Yi responded by feigning illness: 「宣王遂稱疾避爽……宣王密爲之備」[7]. When Cao Shuang left the capital with the young emperor to visit Gaopingling, Sima Yi acted.

According to Pei Songzhi's annotation quoting the *Shiyu*, Sima Yi had Jiang Ji write to Cao Shuang promising that he would only lose office — 「惟免官而已」— swearing by the Luo River; Cao Shuang believed him and disbanded his troops [9], but was then destroyed along with his clan. (Pei's note also records that Jiang Ji, ashamed that his word had been broken, fell ill and died [13].)

q: Who came up with the idea of weighing an elephant by putting it on a boat and marking the waterline?
reply:
**Cao Chong (曹沖, styled Cangshu 倉舒), a son of Cao Cao, came up with this idea.** He was the "Prince Ai of Deng" (鄧哀王). The story is recorded in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (*Sanguozhi*), in the "Biographies of the Sons of Emperor Wu" (魏書·武文世王公傳).

**The account (from Cao Chong's biography):**

At the time, Sun Quan sent a giant elephant, and Cao Cao (魏太祖, "the Grand Ancestor of Wei") wanted to know its weight. He asked his subordinates, but none could come up with a method. Cao Chong said:

「置象大船之上，而刻其水痕所至，稱物以載之，則校可知矣。」[2]

("Put the elephant on a large boat, and carve a mark where the waterline reaches; then weigh things and load them [onto the boat to the same mark], and by comparison [the weight] can be known.")

Cao Cao was delighted and had it carried out at once: 「太祖大悅，卽施行焉。」[2]

**Background on Cao Chong himself (same passage):**

- He was extraordinarily clever as a small child: 「生五六歳，智意所及，有若成人之智。」[2] ("At five or six years old, his intelligence reached that of an adult.")
- Cao Cao often praised him to his ministers and had thoughts of making him his heir: 「太祖數對群臣稱述，有欲傳後意。」[2]
- He died at age thirteen, in the thirteenth year of Jian'an (建安十三年), after an illness; Cao Cao personally prayed for his life: 「年十三，建安十三年疾病，太祖親爲請命。」[2]

A note by Pei Songzhi (裴松之) citing the *Wei Lue* (《魏略》) records that Emperor Wen (Cao Pi) later said: 「若使倉舒在，我亦無天下。」[13] ("Had Cangshu lived, I would not have [come to] possess the empire.")

**My inference:** Based on the passage, the credit belongs to Cao Chong, not to any of Cao Cao's ministers — the text states that when Cao Cao asked his assembled subordinates (訪之群下), they all failed (咸莫能出其理), and it was Cao Chong who supplied the method [2].

q: Who was Boyan? What was his original name?
reply:
**Boyan (伯言) was Lu Xun (陆逊).** 伯言 was his courtesy name (字). His original given name was **Lu Yi (陆议)** — the *Sanguozhi* says his family name was Lu, his courtesy name Boyan, and that his original name was Yi.

**Evidence (from the *Sanguozhi*, Lu Xun's biography):**

- 「陸遜字伯言，吳郡吳人也。本名議，世江東大族。」[1] — "Lu Xun, courtesy name Boyan, a man of Wu county in Wu commandery. His original name was Yi; his family had for generations been a great clan of Jiangdong."

The text also confirms that "Boyan" refers to Lu Xun elsewhere in the book: in Sun Quan's biography, Sun Quan quotes a report that "伯言、承明" (Boyan and Chengming) wept when they met Yuan Li [18], and Zhuge Jin's biography has the speaker address him as 「陸伯言」[13].

**Inference:** From the passage above, "Boyan" and "Lu Xun" are the same person, since the biography states directly that Lu Xun's courtesy name was Boyan; and the original name "Yi" (议) was later changed to "Xun" (逊), though the *Sanguozhi* text here does not state when or why the change was made.

**Following is not a record from the *Sanguozhi*:** The reason usually given for the change of name (avoidance of a naming taboo, etc.) is not stated in the *Sanguozhi*; the text only records 「本名議」.

q: Sun Quan urged one of his generals to study more; later Lu Su was amazed at how much he had learned. Who was this general, and what did he reply to Lu Su?
reply:
## 结论

这位将军是**吕蒙（字子明）**。孙权劝他和蒋钦多读书，吕蒙发奋学习；后来鲁肃接替周瑜、路过吕蒙营屯，与他议论，惊叹他学识大进。吕蒙回答鲁肃的话是：

> 「士別三日，即更刮目相待。大兄今論，何一稱穰侯乎。」[1]

（"读书人分别三天，就该另眼相看。大兄今天这番议论，怎么一再称道穰侯呢。"）

## 依据

**一、孙权劝学、吕蒙发奋**（裴注引《江表传》）：

孙权对吕蒙和蒋钦说「卿今並當塗掌事，宜學問以自開益」；吕蒙推托军中事务繁多，孙权以自己的经历劝勉，并说「宜急讀《孫子》《六韜》《左傳》《國語》及三史」。吕蒙于是「始就學，篤志不倦，其所覽見，舊儒不勝」[1]。

**二、鲁肃惊叹**（裴注引《江表传》）：

「後魯肅上代周瑜，過蒙言議，常欲受屈。肅拊蒙背曰：『吾謂大弟但有武略耳，至於今者，學識英博，非復吳下阿蒙。』」[1] 吕蒙随即以上引「士別三日」一段作答，并接着提醒鲁肃：自己接替周瑜（公瑾）之任，又与关羽为邻，而关羽「長而好學，讀左傳略皆上口，梗亮有雄氣，然性頗自負，好陵人」[1]。

**三、陈寿正文的对应记载**（与裴注情节略异）：

正文记鲁肃接替周瑜赴陆口，路过吕蒙屯下，起初还轻视吕蒙，经人劝说才去拜访。酒酣时吕蒙问他如何防备关羽，鲁肃答「臨時施宜」，吕蒙「因為肅畫五策」。鲁肃于是「越席就之，拊其背曰：『呂子明，吾不知卿才畧所及乃至於此也。』遂拜蒙母，結友而別」[3]。正文这里说的是吕蒙为鲁肃筹划五条策略令其折服，没有出现「士别三日」的对话。

**四、孙权事后的评价**（裴注引《江表传》）：

「權常歎曰：『人長而進益，如呂蒙、蔣欽，蓋不可及也。富貴榮顯，更能折節好學……』」[4]

## 说明

「士别三日，刮目相待」这段对话，出自裴松之注所引的**《江表传》**，不见于陈寿正文；正文只记吕蒙为鲁肃画五策、鲁肃拊背叹服[3]。两处都表明鲁肃对吕蒙的学识/才略刮目相看，但具体情节不同，这里并列说明，不作取舍。

q: Who was the Marquis Shunping (Marquis Who Was Obedient and Peaceful)?
reply:
**The Marquis Shunping was Zhao Yun (Zhao Zilong).** "Shunping" (順平) was the posthumous title granted to him by Liu Shan, the Later Ruler of Shu.

**Who he was**

Zhao Yun, styled Zilong, was a native of Zhending in Changshan commandery. He first served under Gongsun Zan, then followed the First Ruler (Liu Bei) and became his cavalry commander:

> 「趙雲字子龍，常山真定人也。本屬公孫瓚……雲遂隨從，為先主主騎。」[15]

He is most famous for saving Liu Bei's infant son (the future Later Ruler) and Lady Gan at Changban:

> 「及先主為曹公所追於當陽長阪，棄妻子南走，雲身抱弱子，即後主也，保護甘夫人，即後主母也，皆得免難。」[15]

**The title itself**

His biography records that after his death he was granted the posthumous title Shunping:

> 「七年卒，追諡順平侯。」[2]

That is, he died in the seventh year of Jianxing (229 CE), and was posthumously titled Marquis Shunping. The biography also notes that he was one of a group of Shu generals (along with Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, Ma Chao, Pang Tong, and Huang Zhong) who received posthumous titles only in the Later Ruler's reign, which contemporaries regarded as an honor:

> 「於是關羽、張飛、馬超、龐統、黃忠及雲乃追諡，時論以為榮。」[2]

**Why "Shunping"**

Pei Songzhi's commentary quotes the *Yun Bielu* (《雲別傳》), which preserves the Later Ruler's edict and the discussion by Jiang Wei and others. The meaning is explained by the rules of posthumous naming:

> 「謹按諡法，柔賢慈惠曰順，執事有班曰平，克定禍亂曰平，應諡雲曰順平侯。」[1]

So "shun" (順) = "gentle, worthy, kind, and beneficent," and "ping" (平) = "discharging office with order" or "quelling disorder."

**One discrepancy worth noting**

The biography says Zhao Yun died and was titled in Jianxing 7 (229 CE), but the annals of the Later Ruler record the actual bestowal of the posthumous title years later, in Jingyao 4 (261 CE):

> 「四年春三月，追諡故將軍趙雲。」[13]

So the sources differ on the date of the posthumous title: one places it at his death, the other in 261. Pei Songzhi's *Yun Bielu* quotation is attached to the biography's account.

q: Who was called the 'Tiger Fool' (Huchi), and how did he get that nickname?
reply:
**The "Tiger Fool" (虎痴, Huchi) was Xu Chu 許褚, courtesy name Zhongkang 仲康, a strongman and bodyguard of Cao Cao.**

**How he got the name**

The nickname is explained in the *Sanguozhi* right after the account of the standoff with Ma Chao at Tong Pass. Xu Chu's biography says:

「軍中以褚力如虎而痴，故號曰虎痴；是以超問虎侯，至今天下稱焉，皆謂其姓名也。」[1]

(The army called him "Tiger Fool" because his strength was like a tiger's but he was dull-witted; that is why Ma Chao asked about the "Tiger Marquis," and down to today everyone uses it, all taking it for his actual name.)

**Context**

- Xu Chu was a man of Qiao in Qiao Commandery, over eight *chi* tall, with a waist ten spans around, fierce in appearance and of strength surpassing other men; in the late Han he gathered young men and clansmen and fortified his wall against bandits, and even dragged an ox backwards by the tail a hundred paces, so that the people between the Huai, Ru, Chen and Liang regions feared him [2].
- Cao Cao took him on, saying "This is my Fan Kuai," made him a Commandant the same day, and kept him as a bodyguard; his followers became "Tiger Warriors" (虎士) [3].
- At Tong Pass, when Cao Cao met Han Sui and Ma Chao for a single-horse parley with only Xu Chu attending, Ma Chao wanted to rush and seize Cao Cao but was deterred by Xu Chu glaring at him. Ma Chao had heard of Xu Chu's bravery and suspected the rider with Cao Cao was he, so he asked Cao Cao: 「公有虎侯者安在？」— "Where is the one they call Tiger Marquis?" [3]. It is from this "Tiger Marquis" (虎侯) that the epithet "Tiger Fool" (虎痴) is explained.

So the name is essentially a soldier's nickname: tiger-strength plus a simple, dull manner. The biography adds that Xu Chu was cautious, law-abiding, plain and of few words [4].

**Note**

This is *not* the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* invention — the nickname 虎痴 is in Chen Shou's text itself [1].

q: Li Tien voluntarily moved his clan and retainers to Yeh. How many people did he move in total, and which Han-dynasty figure did Ts'ao Ts'ao tease him about?
reply:
**答案：** 李典（Li Dian，字曼成）把部曲、宗族共 **一万三千多口** 迁到邺城；曹操拿东汉的 **耿纯（Geng Chun）** 来打趣他。

**依据：**

1. 李典的宗族、部曲本来住在乘氏，他主动请求迁到魏郡（邺属魏郡）：

> 「典宗族部曲三千餘家，居乘氏，自請原徙詣魏郡。」[2]

这里说的是 **三千余家**，曹操听后笑着问他：

> 「太祖笑曰：『卿欲慕耿純邪？』」[2]

李典回答说，自己是因为「爵寵過厚」「征伐未息」，应当「實郊遂之內，以制四方」，并非仰慕耿纯：

> 「典謝曰：『典駑怯功微，而爵寵過厚，誠宜舉宗陳力；加以征伐未息，宜實郊遂之內，以制四方，非慕純也。』」[2]

2. 迁移完成后，正文给出了总人数和去向：

> 「遂徙部曲宗族萬三千餘口居鄴。」[1]

曹操为此嘉奖他，升他为破虏将军：

> 「太祖嘉之，遷破虜將軍。」[1]

**推断：** 据 [2]，请求迁移时李典的宗族部曲是「三千餘家」，而 [1] 记实际迁走的是「萬三千餘口」——据此推断，「三千餘家」是按户数计，一万三千余口是按人口计，二者是同一批人的两种算法（一家平均约四口余），而非前后两次迁移。原文只记了这两处数字，没有明说二者关系，这一点是我的推断。

**以下不是《三国志》的记载：** 《三国志》此处只提到「耿純」这个名字（曹操的玩笑和李典的答语），并未在本篇里交代耿纯的朝代和事迹；若说耿纯是东汉开国时率宗族归附光武帝的人物，那是本篇正文之外的背景知识，不在所查这段记载里。

q: How many sons did Cao Cao have in total?
reply:
**结论：据《三国志·魏书·武文世王公传》开篇的统计，曹操共有二十五个儿子。**

原文明确记载：

「武皇帝二十五男：卞皇后生文皇帝、任城威王彰、陳思王植、蕭懷王熊；劉夫人生豐愍王昂、相殤王鑠；環夫人生鄧哀王衝、彭城王據、燕王宇；杜夫人生沛穆王林、中山恭王衮；秦夫人生濟陽懷王玹、陳留恭王峻；尹夫人生范陽閔王矩；王昭儀生趙王幹；孫姬生臨邑殤公子上、楚王彪、剛殤公子勤；李姬生谷城殤公子乘、郿戴公子整、靈殤公子京；周姬生樊安公均；劉姬生廣宗殤公子棘；宋姬生東平靈王徽；趙姬生樂陵王茂。」[4]

按生母分列，这二十五人是：

- 卞皇后所生（4人）：曹丕（文皇帝）、曹彰、曹植、曹熊
- 刘夫人所生（2人）：曹昂、曹铄
- 环夫人所生（3人）：曹冲、曹据、曹宇
- 杜夫人所生（2人）：曹林、曹衮
- 秦夫人所生（2人）：曹玹、曹峻
- 尹夫人所生（1人）：曹矩
- 王昭仪所生（1人）：曹幹
- 孙姬所生（3人）：曹上、曹彪、曹勤
- 李姬所生（3人）：曹乘、曹整、曹京
- 周姬所生（1人）：曹均
- 刘姬所生（1人）：曹棘
- 宋姬所生（1人）：曹徽
- 赵姬所生（1人）：曹茂

q: Whose daughter was Diaochan, and how did she drive a wedge between Dong Zhuo and Lü Bu?
reply:
**Conclusion first:** In the *Sanguozhi* (Records of the Three Kingdoms) there is **no Diaochan**. Chen Shou never records anyone named Diaochan, and never says she was anyone's daughter — not Wang Yun's, not anyone's. The "Diaochan" who is Wang Yun's adopted daughter / singing girl and who seduces first Lü Bu and then Dong Zhuo is a figure from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* (and earlier popular drama), not from the histories.

What the *Sanguozhi* does record is a wedge driven between Dong Zhuo and Lü Bu by two things: Dong Zhuo's own violence toward Lü Bu, and Lü Bu's secret affair with one of Dong Zhuo's maidservants.

**The evidence (quotes in the original, with paraphrase):**

1. Lü Bu's own biography records the hand-halberd incident and the affair:
「卓自以遇人無禮，恐人謀己，行止常以布自衛。然卓性剛而褊，忿不思難，嘗小失意，拔手戟擲布。布拳捷避之，為卓顧謝，卓意亦解。由是陰怨卓。卓常使布守中閤，布與卓侍婢私通，恐事發覺，心不自安。」[18]
Dong Zhuo knew he treated people rudely and feared plots, so he kept Lü Bu as his bodyguard wherever he went; but being harsh and narrow, he once threw a hand-halberd at Lü Bu in anger. Lü Bu dodged it and apologized, and Dong Zhuo's anger passed — but from then on Lü Bu secretly resented him. Dong Zhuo often had Lü Bu guard his inner chambers, and Lü Bu carried on an illicit affair with one of Dong Zhuo's maidservants (侍婢), and fearing discovery, was uneasy. Note: this is **"a maidservant," unnamed — no name, no parentage, no "daughter of" anyone.**

2. Wang Yun's cultivation of Lü Bu and the recruitment as inside man:
「先是，司徒王允以布州里壯健，厚接納之。後布詣允，陳卓幾見殺狀。時允與僕射士孫瑞密謀誅卓，是以告布使為內應。布曰：『奈如父子何！』允曰：『君自姓呂，本非骨肉。今憂死不暇，何謂父子？』布遂許之，手刃刺卓。」[11]
Earlier, Wang Yun — because Lü Bu was a strong man from his own region — had treated him generously. Later Lü Bu came to Wang Yun and described how Dong Zhuo had nearly killed him. Wang Yun, who was secretly plotting with the director Shisun Rui to kill Dong Zhuo, therefore told Lü Bu to act as an inside man. Lü Bu objected, "What about the father-and-son bond?" Wang Yun replied, "Your surname is Lü; you were never flesh and blood. You can't even save your own life — what father and son?" Lü Bu agreed and personally stabbed Dong Zhuo to death.

3. The conspiracy and killing, dated:
「三年四月，司徒王允、尚書僕射士孫瑞、卓將呂布共謀誅卓。」[14] — In the fourth month of the third year (of the Chuping era), Wang Yun, Shisun Rui, and Dong Zhuo's own officer Lü Bu plotted together to kill Dong Zhuo. 「布曰『有詔』，遂殺卓」[14] — Lü Bu said "There is an edict," and so killed Dong Zhuo.

**Inference (marked as such):** From these facts we can see how the rupture actually worked, without any woman playing a double game. First, Dong Zhuo had made Lü Bu his sworn "son" (「誓為父子」[13]); second, Dong Zhuo threw a weapon at Lü Bu and nearly killed him, so Lü Bu bore secret resentment [18]; third, Lü Bu was committing adultery with a woman in Dong Zhuo's household and was afraid of being caught [18]; fourth, Lü Bu poured all this out to Wang Yun, who was already plotting against Dong Zhuo and had long been courting Lü Bu [11]. So: Lü Bu's fear and resentment, plus Wang Yun's existing conspiracy, were enough to turn him. The illicit affair with the maidservant is a genuine historical element; what the histories do not supply is her name, her being Wang Yun's daughter, or her acting deliberately to split the two men.

**Background — this is not from the *Sanguozhi*:**
The claim that Diaochan was Wang Yun's daughter (or adopted daughter / singing girl), and that she deliberately set Dong Zhuo and Lü Bu against each other, is not recorded in the *Sanguozhi*; it comes from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* or other non-orthodox (non-historical) accounts. In the *Sanguozhi* the woman involved is only called Dong Zhuo's 「侍婢」 — an unnamed maidservant.

One caution: the word 「貂蟬」 does appear once in the *Sanguozhi*, but it is not a name — it is part of the official title 「貂蟬內侍」, referring to an attendant office at court [1]. It has nothing to do with the fictional character.

q: How old was Lü Tai when he died, and in which year did he die?
reply:
**Conclusion:** 《三国志》 has no record of anyone named **呂泰 (Lü Tai)**. The figure matching your question is almost certainly **呂岱 (Lü Dai)**, courtesy name 定公, of 廣陵海陵 — he died at the age of **96**, in **太平元年**, which is **256 AD** (Sun Wu's 太平 era, under the Wu ruler Sun Liang).

**Evidence:**

「太平元年，年九十六卒，子凱嗣。」[7]

(The same passage adds that he left orders for a plain coffin and coarse cloth, with the funeral kept frugal — 「遣令殯以素棺，疏巾布褠，葬送之制，務從儉約，凱皆奉行之」[7].)

His career context in the biography: he served Sun Quan from his early days in the 幕府, campaigned in 長沙 and 交州 (where he executed 士徽 and was enfeoffed as 番禺侯), and under Sun Liang was appointed 大司馬 — 「孫亮即位，拜大司馬」[13]. By then he was already over eighty and still vigorous: 「時年已八十，然體素精勤，躬親王事」[13].

So: age 96 at death, in 太平元年 = 256 AD.

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:** The name 呂泰 does not appear in the 《三国志》 text or Pei Songzhi's commentary; the Wu general who died at 96 in 太平元年 is 呂岱. 廣陵海陵 (his native place) is in present-day Jiangsu Province.

q: When I Chi went as an envoy to Wu, Sun Ch'üan deliberately asked him whether serving an unprincipled lord was tiring. How did I Chi reply?
reply:
**结论**：孙权问「勞事無道之君乎？」——侍奉无道的君主辛苦吗？伊籍回答：「一拜一起，未足為勞。」意思是：不过一拜一起罢了，算不得辛苦。他既没有承认自己是在"辛苦侍奉无道之君"，又借"一拜一起"把礼数说成只是入见时的叩拜，避开正面回答，还暗含机锋。孙权因此觉得他很不一般。

**依据**（《三国志·蜀书·许糜孙简伊秦传》伊籍本传）：

- 伊籍字机伯，山阳人，先依附刘表，刘表死后随先主南渡长江、入益州；益州平定后任左将军从事中郎，「遣東使于吳」[1]——即被派往东吴出使。
- 「孫權聞其才辨，欲逆折以辭。籍適入拜，權曰︰『勞事無道之君乎？』籍即對曰︰『一拜一起，未足為勞。』」[1]
- 「籍之機捷，類皆如此，權甚異之。」[1]（伊籍的机敏便捷大多如此，孙权觉得他很不同寻常。）
- 同传还记他后来「遷昭文將軍，與諸葛亮、法正、劉巴、李嚴共造《蜀科》」[1]。

**推断**：据「欲逆折以辭」[1]，孙权这一问是有意刁难、想在言辞上压倒伊籍；而「一拜一起，未足為勞」[1]把"劳"的范围缩小到一次入见的拜起，据此推断，伊籍是用偷换"侍奉"与"一拜一起"的方式避开了"无道之君"的陷阱，既不失礼、也不顺着孙权的话贬损自己的君主。

（此事的年份，本传原文没有记在这件事上，故不写公元年。）

q: Ts'ao Ts'ao asked P'ei Ch'ien about Liu Pei's abilities. How did P'ei Ch'ien assess him?
reply:
**Answer:** When Cao Cao asked Pei Qian how he rated Liu Bei's ability and judgment, Pei Qian replied that if Liu Bei were placed in the Central Plains (the heartland), he could throw it into disorder but could not govern it; if he took advantage of an opening and held a strategic defensible position, he could become the lord of one region.

**Evidence**

The exchange is recorded in Pei Qian's biography in the *Wei Shu*:

- Cao Cao asked: 「卿前與劉備俱在荊州，卿以備才略何如？」 [3] — "You were formerly together with Liu Bei in Jing province; how do you rate Liu Bei's ability and judgment?"
- Pei Qian answered: 「使居中國，能亂人而不能爲治也。若乘閒守險，足以爲一方主。」 [3] — "Put him in the Central Plains, and he can bring disorder to people but cannot govern them. If he seizes an opening and holds a strategic position, he is sufficient to be the lord of one region."

**Context from the same passage:** Pei Qian (Pei Qian, courtesy name Wenxing), a man of Wenxi in Hedong, had fled the disorders to Jing province, where Liu Biao treated him as an honored guest. Pei Qian privately told those close to him, Wang Can and Sima Zhi, that "Liu Mu [Liu Biao] is not a man of hegemon-king talent, yet wishes to style himself as the Western Count [i.e., a virtuous ruler]; his defeat will not be long in coming" — 「劉牧非霸王之才，乃欲西伯自處，其敗無日矣。」 [3] He then went south to Changsha. After Cao Cao (the Grand Ancestor / 太祖) pacified Jing province, he appointed Pei Qian to serve on the staff of the Chancellor's military affairs [3]. It was in this context that Cao Cao put the question to him, since Pei Qian had earlier been in Jing province at the same time as Liu Bei.

**Note on the text:** The passage appears in the *Wei Shu* (Book of Wei), in the joint biography of He, Chang, Yang, Du, Zhao, and Pei (chapter 23 of the *Sanguozhi*). The names in the question correspond to Cao Cao (Ts'ao Ts'ao), Pei Qian (P'ei Ch'ien), and Liu Bei (Liu Pei).

q: Zhongli Mu, as Grand Administrator of Wuling, put down a rebellion of the Five Streams tribes stirred up by Guo Chun, an agent sent by Wei. In which year was this, and how many troops did he have?
reply:
**Short answer:** This happened in **263 CE** (the sixth year of the Sun Wu era Yong'an 永安), and Zhongli Mu (钟离牧) went in with **only 3,000 troops**.

**Evidence**

- The date and the whole episode are in Zhongli Mu's biography. The text opens with the year:

  「永安六年，蜀併於魏，武陵五谿夷與蜀接界。時論懼叛亂，乃以牧為平魏將軍，領武陵太守，往之郡。魏遣漢葭縣長郭純試守武陵太守，率涪陵民入蜀遷陵界，屯於赤沙，誘致諸夷邑君，或起應純，又進攻酉陽縣，郡中震懼。」[1]

  ("In the sixth year of Yong'an, Shu was annexed by Wei... Wei sent Guo Chun, chief of Hanjia county, to act as Grand Administrator of Wuling; he led the people of Fuling into the Qianling border area of Shu, camped at Chisha, lured the Yi chiefs, some of whom rose to answer him, and attacked Youyang county; the commandery was shaken with fear.")

  The year Yong'an 6 = **263 CE** (converted with the era tool).

- The size of his force is stated in the objection raised by the General Who Pacifies the Yi, Gao Shang:

  「撫夷將軍高尚說牧曰：『昔潘太常督兵五萬，然後以討五谿夷耳……而明府以三千兵深入，尚未見其利也。』牧曰：『非常之事，何得循舊？』即率所領，晨夜進道，緣山險行，垂二千里……純等散，五谿平。」[1]

  ("Gao Shang said: 'Formerly Grand Constant Attendant Pan commanded 50,000 troops before he could attack the Five Streams Yi... yet you, my lord, go deep in with 3,000 troops, and I do not yet see the advantage.' Mu replied: 'Extraordinary affairs—how can one follow old precedents?' He at once led his command, marching day and night, along the mountain defiles for nearly two thousand li... Guo Chun and the others scattered, and the Five Streams were pacified.")

**On the numbers:** The 3,000 is the force Zhongli Mu actually led in (the figure given in Gao Shang's warning, which the narrative bears out). Note that this was explicitly *not* a large expeditionary army: the comparison drawn is with the earlier campaign of Grand Constant Attendant Pan (潘濬), who is said to have had 50,000. The same passage is echoed in Pei Songzhi's commentary quoting the *Kuaiji Dianlu* (《會稽典錄》), where Zhongli Mu recalls the small forces he had been given: 「大皇帝时，陆丞相讨鄱阳，以二千人授吾，潘太常讨武陵，吾又有三千人」[11] — i.e. 2,000 men for Lu Xun's Poyang campaign and 3,000 for Pan Jun's Wuling campaign, underlining his habitual shortage of troops.

**One point of wording:** the source says the court appointed him **acting Grand Administrator of Wuling** by making him "General Who Pacifies Wei, concurrently Grand Administrator of Wuling" (「以牧為平魏將軍，領武陵太守」[1]), and that he later "again, as General of the Front holding the tally, concurrently served as Grand Administrator of Wuling" (「復以前將軍假節，領武陵太守」[1]) — so "Grand Administrator of Wuling" is right, but his formal post was a concurrent (領) one held alongside a general's title.

q: When Liu Bei was gravely ill, Huang Yuan, the Grand Administrator of Hanjia, rebelled and burned Linqiong. How did Yang Hong work out where Huang Yuan would go, and how was he captured?
reply:
**Conclusion:** Yang Hong (楊洪) reasoned not from any report of Huang Yuan's movements but from Huang Yuan's character. He argued that Huang Yuan, being by nature fierce and violent and enjoying no goodwill or loyalty from others, could never manage the ambitious plan of seizing Nanzhong through Yuexi that everyone else feared; instead he would simply flee downstream by boat, hoping either that the ruler recovered — in which case he would bind himself and come back to die — or that the ruler died, in which case he would run to Wu to save his life. On that basis Yang Hong ordered the pursuit to wait at the mouth of the Nan'an gorge, and Huang Yuan was taken alive there. [1]

**The reasoning and the capture**

Yang Hong's biography records the whole episode: 「漢嘉太守黃元素為諸葛亮所不善，聞先主疾病，懼有後患，舉郡反，燒臨邛城。時亮東行省疾，成都單虛，是以元益無所憚。洪即啟太子，遣其親兵，使將軍陳曶、鄭綽討元。」 [1] — Huang Yuan had long been disliked by Zhuge Liang; hearing of the First Ruler's illness he feared future trouble, raised his commandery in revolt and burned Linqiong; with Zhuge Liang away east visiting the sick, Chengdu was empty, so Yuan was the less deterred. Yang Hong reported to the Crown Prince and sent his personal troops under the generals Chen Hu (陳曶) and Zheng Chuo (鄭綽) against Yuan.

The council of others, and Yang Hong's rebuttal: 「眾議以為元若不能圍成都，當由越囗據南中。洪曰：『元素信凶暴，無他恩信，何能辦此？不過乘水東下，冀主上平安，面縛歸死；如其有異，奔吳求活耳。敕曶、綽但於南安峽口遮即便得矣。』」 [1] — everyone assumed that failing to besiege Chengdu, Yuan would go by way of Yuexi to seize Nanzhong; Yang Hong said Yuan, "by nature truly fierce and violent, with no other goodwill or trust," could not accomplish that — he would only ride the water downstream, hoping the sovereign would recover and he could tie himself up and come to die, or, if things turned out otherwise, flee to Wu to seek survival — so Chen Hu and Zheng Chuo need only block him at the mouth of the Nan'an gorge.

The result: 「曶、綽承洪言，果生獲元。」 [1] — they followed Yang Hong's words and did capture Yuan alive.

**The date, and the other account of the capture**

The First Ruler's biography dates it: 「三年春二月，丞相亮自成都到永安。三月，黃元進兵攻臨邛縣。遣將軍陳曶討元，元軍敗，順流下江，為其親兵所縛，生致成都，斬之。」 [13] — in the third year (Zhangwu 3 = 223 AD), third month, Huang Yuan advanced on Linqiong county; general Chen Hu was sent against him, Yuan's army was defeated and went downstream, and he was bound by his own personal soldiers and delivered alive to Chengdu, where he was beheaded. Liu Bei died in the fourth month of that same year, aged sixty-three. [13]

Note that the two accounts differ slightly: Yang Hong's biography says Chen Hu and Zheng Chuo took Yuan alive at the gorge [1], while the First Ruler's biography says his army was beaten, he went downstream, and his own personal troops bound him and delivered him to Chengdu, where he was executed [13]. Both agree that Yang Hong's prediction of the route and the interception was what produced the capture.

q: A soldier who went out and never came back was treated as a deserter, and his wife and children were made government slaves. His wife protested everywhere without success. Which Commandant of Justice eventually discovered that the soldier had been murdered for money by a man from his own camp, and who was the murderer?
reply:
**Answer:** The Commandant of Justice (廷尉) was **Gao Rou 高柔 (Gao Wen Hui 高文惠)**, and the murderer was **Jiao Ziwen 焦子文**, a fellow soldier in Dou Li's own camp (護軍營).

**The case as recorded in the *Sanguozhi* (in the biography of Gao Rou, *Wei Shu* 24):**

The soldier **Dou Li 窦礼** went out and did not return. His camp treated him as a deserter, petitioned to hunt him down, and confiscated his wife **Ying 盈** and their children as government slaves:

> 「頃之，護軍營士竇禮近出不還。營以為亡，表言逐捕，沒其妻盈及男女為官奴婢。盈連至州府，稱冤自訟，莫有省者。乃辭詣廷尉。」[1]

*(Shortly after, the soldier Dou Li of the Protector's camp went out and did not come back. The camp took him for a deserter, petitioned to pursue and arrest him, and confiscated his wife Ying and their children as government slaves. Ying went repeatedly to the provincial authorities, crying that she had been wronged and pleading her own case, but no one paid attention; so she appealed to the Commandant of Justice.)*

Gao Rou questioned her. She said her husband was not the sort to abandon his family; asked about quarrels and money, she replied that he had lent money to a fellow soldier of the same camp, Jiao Ziwen, and had not been able to get it back:

> 「又曰：『汝夫不與人交錢財乎？』對曰：『嘗出錢與同營士焦子文，求不得。』」[1]

Jiao Ziwen happened then to be jailed on a minor matter. Gao Rou saw him and trapped him: first Jiao denied ever borrowing anyone's money, then Gao Rou caught the change in his expression and pressed him:

> 「柔察子文色動，遂曰：『汝昔舉竇禮錢，何言不邪？』……柔曰：『汝已殺禮，便宜早服。』子文於是叩頭，具首殺禮本末，埋藏處所。」[1]

*(Gao Rou noticed Jiao Ziwen's expression change, and said: "You formerly borrowed Dou Li's money — why do you say you did not?" … Gao Rou said: "You have already killed Dou Li; you had best confess early." Jiao Ziwen then knocked his head on the ground and fully confessed the whole course of the killing and the place of burial.)*

Gao Rou sent officers and soldiers to dig at the spot indicated and recovered the body, and an edict restored Ying and her children to commoner status:

> 「柔便遣吏卒，承子文辭往掘禮，即得其屍。詔書復盈母子為平民。」[1]

That Gao Rou held the office of Commandant of Justice is stated in his biography: 「四年，遷為廷尉」[28] (in the fourth year [of Huangchu] he was promoted to Commandant of Justice) — the Dou Li case is recorded during his tenure in that office.

**So:** the official who uncovered the truth was **Gao Rou, the Commandant of Justice**, and the murderer was **Jiao Ziwen**, who had killed Dou Li over money (the loan) and buried the body.

q: Which Cavalier Regular Palace Attendant of Wu got drunk and collapsed at the banquet Sun Hao held for Ding Zhong on his return from an embassy to Jin, and was beheaded in the hall on Sun Hao's orders? In which year?
reply:
## Answer

The man was **Wang Fan 王蕃** (courtesy name Yongyuan 永元, of Lujiang). He held the office of **Cavalier Regular Palace Attendant (散騎中常侍)**, and he was beheaded in the hall on Sun Hao's orders at the great banquet Sun Hao held when Ding Zhong returned from his embassy to Jin.

**Year: 甘露二年 (the 2nd year of the Ganlu era of Wu) = AD 266.**

### Evidence

The main account is in the *Wang Fan* section of the *Wu Shu*:

「甘露二年，丁忠使晉還，皓大會群臣，蕃沉醉頓伏。皓疑而不悅，舉蕃出外。頃之請還，酒亦不解。蕃性有威嚴，行止自若，皓大怒，呵左右於殿下斬之。衛將軍滕牧、征西將軍留平請，不能得。」[1]

*("In the 2nd year of Ganlu, when Ding Zhong returned from his mission to Jin, Hao held a great assembly of the assembled ministers. Fan was dead drunk and collapsed. Hao grew suspicious and displeased, and had Fan carried outside. After a while Fan asked to return, his drunkenness still not gone. Fan was by nature dignified, and his bearing was as usual; Hao flew into a rage and shouted to his attendants to behead him below the hall. General of the Guards Teng Mu and General of the Western Conquest Liu Ping interceded for him, but could not obtain a pardon.")*

His office is confirmed by his biography's opening block: 「孫休即位，與賀邵、薛瑩、虞汜俱為散騎中常侍，皆加駙馬都尉」[14] — under Sun Xiu he and He Shao, Xue Ying and Yu Si all served as Cavalier Regular Palace Attendants, each with the added title of Commandant of the Cavalier Attendants.

His age and the aftermath: 「蕃死時年三十九，皓徙蕃家屬廣州」[13] — he was 39 when he died, and Sun Hao deported his family to Guangzhou.

The date of the embassy is given in Sun Hao's annals: 「寶鼎元年正月，遣大鴻臚張儼、五官中郎將丁忠弔祭晉文帝」[3] — in the 1st month of the 1st year of Baoding, Zhang Yan and Ding Zhong were sent to offer condolences on the death of Emperor Wen of Jin. The banquet and execution are dated 甘露二年 [1], which the era converter gives as AD 266.

### Note on a variant account (Pei Songzhi's commentary)

Pei Songzhi records a differing version. Pei's commentary quotes the *Jiangbiao Zhuan*: 「皓用巫史之言，谓建业宫不利，乃西巡武昌……問蕃『射不主皮，為力不同科，其義云何』？蕃思惟未答，即於殿上斬蕃」 — Sun Hao, on the advice of shamans and astrologers, went west to Wuchang intending to move the capital, and fearing the ministers would object he held a great banquet, where he questioned Wang Fan on a passage from the *Analects* and beheaded him on the spot when he hesitated; the text itself adds 「此與本傳不同」 (this differs from the main biography). Pei's commentary also quotes the *Wu Lu*'s version of the banquet taunting. Pei Songzhi's own note (臣松之按) points out that the *Wu Lu* account is inconsistent: Ding Zhong returned from the north in the spring of that year, whereas Wan Yu did not become Chancellor until the autumn, so the two accounts do not agree.

I follow the main biography for the circumstances (drunk and collapsing at the banquet) as you asked; the *Jiangbiao Zhuan* gives a different occasion and cause.

---

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:** The *Jiangbiao Zhuan* and *Wu Lu* versions quoted above come from Pei Songzhi's commentary, not Chen Shou's main text.

q: During the Incident at the Gaoping Tombs, when Sima Yi removed Cao Shuang, which two ministers did he send to take over the camps of Cao Shuang and Cao Xi respectively, and what did Sima Yi say to one of them?
reply:
## 结论

在嘉平元年（高平陵之变）中，司马懿（司马宣王）罢免曹爽时，派去接管两处军营的是：

- **高柔（Gao Rou）**——接管曹爽本人的军营。皇太后下诏召高柔，让他「假节行大将军」（持节代理大将军职事），占据曹爽的营。司马懿对他说的一句话是：**「君为周勃矣。」**（"You are now Zhou Bo."）

- **王观（Wang Guan）**——接管曹爽之弟曹羲的军营。司马懿让他「行中领军」（代理中领军），占据曹羲的营。

## 依据

关于高柔：

「太傅司馬宣王奏免曹爽，皇太後詔召柔假節行大將軍事，據爽營。太傅謂柔曰：『君為周勃矣。』」[16]

（Sima Yi memorialized to remove Cao Shuang; the Empress Dowager issued an edict summoning Gao Rou, granting him the tally and having him act as Grand General to occupy Cao Shuang's camp. The Grand Tutor said to Rou, "You are now Zhou Bo."）

关于王观：

「司馬宣王誅爽，使觀行中領軍，據爽弟羲營」[23]

（Sima Yi, in executing Cao Shuang, made Wang Guan act as the Central Commander of the Army [中領軍] and occupy the camp of Shuang's younger brother Cao Xi.）

关于曹羲的身份，可作旁证——他正是曹爽之弟、时任中领军：「爽弟羲為中領軍」[9]，所以「行中领军，据羲营」即是以代理中领军之名接管曹羲所领之营。

## 推断

据此推断：司马懿对高柔说的「君为周勃矣」，是把高柔比作西汉的周勃——周勃曾在吕后死后与陈平合谋，一举诛灭诸吕、安定汉室。司马懿以此语，是把这次夺曹爽之兵、清除曹爽集团的行动类比于周勃安刘之举，意在称许并勉励高柔。不过这只是一种比拟措辞，原文并未明说高柔具体做了什么。

（司马懿称高柔接管曹爽营、王观接管曹羲营，均是「占据军营」的军事接管动作，因此二人分别对应曹爽、曹羲两营，与问题所问相符。）

q: What happened when Zhuge Liang used the Empty Fort Strategy at Yangping to scare off Sima Yi?
reply:
## Conclusion

The "Empty Fort" episode at Yangping **is not in Chen Shou's main text (正文) of the *Sanguo zhi* at all**. It survives only in a quotation from Guo Chong's 郭沖《三事》, embedded in Pei Songzhi's commentary to the *Zhuge Liang zhuan* — and the very same commentary block immediately refutes it. So the standard answer is: the story as you tell it is a piece of anecdote that Pei Songzhi himself judged false.

## What the anecdote says (裴注引郭沖《三事》)

「亮屯于陽平，遣魏延諸軍並兵東下，亮惟留萬人守城。晉宣帝率二十萬眾拒亮，而與延軍錯道，徑至前，當亮六十里所，偵候白宣帝說亮在城中兵少力弱。……亮意氣自若，敕軍中皆臥旗息鼓，不得妄出菴幔，又令大開四城門，埽地卻洒。宣帝常謂亮持重，而猥見勢弱，疑其有伏兵，於是引軍北趣山。」[1]

("Zhuge Liang was camped at Yangping; he sent Wei Yan and the other armies east together, keeping only ten thousand men to hold the city. Emperor Xuan [Sima Yi] came against him with two hundred thousand troops, but missed Wei Yan's column by a different road and came straight on to within about sixty *li*. Zhuge Liang ordered banners down and drums silent, no one to leave the tents, and had all four city gates thrown open and the ground swept and sprinkled. Emperor Xuan, who always thought Zhuge Liang careful and heavy, suddenly seeing him show weakness, suspected an ambush and led his army north to the hills.") It goes on to record Zhuge Liang laughing the next day, saying Sima Yi must have thought him cowardly and suspected a strong ambush, and Sima Yi later regretting it deeply [1].

## Why it is rejected — the refutation in the same commentary

The text appended to the same block (the 難 / Pei Songzhi's own note) argues:

「案陽平在漢中。亮初屯陽平，宣帝尚為荊州都督，鎮宛城，至曹真死後，始與亮於關中相抗禦耳。魏嘗遣宣帝自宛由西城伐蜀，值霖雨，不果。此之前後，無復有於陽平交兵事。就如沖言，宣帝既舉二十萬眾，已知亮兵少力弱，若疑其有伏兵，正可設防持重，何至便走乎？」[1]

("Yangping is in Hanzhong. When Zhuge Liang first camped at Yangping, Emperor Xuan was still Governor of Jingzhou, stationed at Wancheng; only after Cao Zhen's death did he begin to confront Zhuge Liang in the Guanzhong region. Wei once sent Emperor Xuan from Wan by way of Xicheng to attack Shu, but continuous rain stopped it. Before and after this, there was no engagement at Yangping. Even granting Guo Chong's account — since Emperor Xuan had already learned Zhuge Liang was weak, if he suspected an ambush he could simply have taken up defensive precautions; why flee outright?")

A further note adds:

「案《魏延傳》云：『延每隨亮出，輒欲請精兵萬人，與亮異道會于潼關，亮制而不許；延常謂亮為怯，歎己才用之不盡也。』亮尚不以延為萬人別統，豈得如沖言，頓使將重兵在前，而以輕弱自守乎？且沖與扶風王言，顯彰宣帝之短，對子毀父，理所不容，而云『扶風王慨然善沖之言』，故知此書舉引皆虛。」[22]

("The *Wei Yan zhuan* says Wei Yan repeatedly asked to take ten thousand picked troops and meet Zhuge Liang at Tong Pass by a separate road, and Zhuge Liang restrained him and would not allow it. If Zhuge Liang would not even let Wei Yan command ten thousand separately, how could he, as Guo Chong says, have suddenly put heavy troops in the front under Wei Yan and kept only the weak to defend himself? Moreover, Guo Chong told this to the Prince of Fufeng, plainly to expose Emperor Xuan's shortcoming — slandering the father to the son, which is intolerable; yet he claims 'the Prince of Fufeng praised Guo Chong's words with emotion.' Hence we know the citations in this book are all false.")

## Inferred conclusion

Pulling these facts together: (a) the only source for the empty-fort trick is Guo Chong's *Sanshi*, quoted in Pei's commentary [1]; (b) Pei Songzhi's own note shows the geography and chronology do not fit — when Zhuge Liang was at Yangping, Sima Yi was still in Jingzhou/Wancheng, and they only faced each other in Guanzhong after Cao Zhen's death [1]; (c) the *Wei Yan zhuan* contradicts the premise that Zhuge Liang would leave Wei Yan with the main force while keeping himself weak [22]. Therefore, on the *Sanguo zhi*'s own testimony, this episode should not be treated as historical fact; Chen Shou's main narrative of Zhuge Liang's campaigns (祁山, 陈仓, 街亭, 武都阴平) contains no such scene [20][15].

## Background (not from the *Sanguo zhi* text proper)

What you call the "Empty Fort Strategy" (*kongcheng ji*) is chiefly known from the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* and stage tradition; the *Sanguo zhi*'s main text has no such episode, and the one anecdote resembling it, in Pei Songzhi's commentary, is there quoted only to be refuted. Yangping (阳平) is in the Hanzhong region, in present-day Shaanxi province.

q: Who were the 'Eight Masters of Wu', and what was each of them famous for?
reply:
## Who they were

The group recorded in the *Sanguozhi* is called the **八絕 ("Eight Excellences")**, not "Eight Masters" — the list comes from Pei Songzhi's note quoting the *Wulu* (《吳錄》), appended to the biography of Zhao Da:

> 「皇象字休明，廣陵江都人。幼工書……嚴武字子卿，衞尉畯再從子也，圍棊莫與爲輩。宋壽占夢，十不失一。曹不興善畫，權使畫屏风，誤落筆點素，因就以作蠅……孤城鄭嫗能相人，及範、惇、達八人，世皆稱妙，謂之八絕云。」[11]

The eight, with what each was known for:

1. **Huang Xiang 皇象** (zi Xiuming), of Jiangdu, Guangling — **calligraphy**. "幼工書" (skilled at writing from youth); he is said to have balanced the excesses of his contemporaries Zhang Zibing (too slack) and Chen Liangfu (too taut), so that "中國善書者不能及也" [11].
2. **Yan Wu 嚴武** (zi Ziqing), a junior kinsman of the Commandant of the Guards Yan Jun — **the board game weiqi/go**: "圍棊莫與爲輩" (no one was his peer at go) [11].
3. **Song Shou 宋壽** — **dream interpretation**: "占夢，十不失一" (he read dreams and was not wrong once in ten) [11].
4. **Cao Buxing 曹不興** — **painting**. Sun Quan had him paint a screen; he accidentally dropped a dot of ink on the silk and turned it into a fly, which Sun Quan took for a live fly and brushed at: "權以爲生蠅，舉手彈之" [11].
5. **Zheng Yu 鄭嫗** of Gucheng — **physiognomy**: "能相人" (could read a person's face/fate) [11].
6. **Wu Fan 吳範** (zi Wenze), of Shangyu, Kuaiji — **calendrical/astrological divination and reading of "wind-and-qi" omens**: "以治曆數知風氣聞於郡中"; "每有災祥，輒推數言狀。其術多效" [67]. He predicted the capture of Huang Zu, that Liu Bei would gain Yi province, and the taking of Guan Yu: "明日日中" — Guan Yu was in fact taken, "須臾，外稱萬歲，傳言得羽" [70]. Sun Quan made him Commandant of Cavalry and acting Director of the Grand Astrologer (騎都尉，領太史令) [75].
7. **Liu Dun 劉惇** (zi Ziren), of Pingyuan — **the "celestial offices" (天官) and divination by numbers**: "以明天官達占數顯於南土。每有水旱寇賊，皆先時處期，無不中者", so Sun Fu made him army adviser and the army called him "the divine" (神明) [73]. He was especially strong in the *Taiyi* method, wrote over a hundred chapters, and was praised by the scholar Diao Xuan [81].
8. **Zhao Da 趙達** — **arithmetical/astrological calculation (推算)**. Sun Quan had him calculate before campaigns and "皆如其言" [62]; he predicted the length of Sun Quan's reign [63]. He refused to reveal his method and took it to the grave: Sun Quan seized his daughter to get his book, but "發棺無所得，法術絕焉" [62].

Note that **Zhang Zibing 張子並** and **Chen Liangfu 陳梁甫** are also named in the same note as skilled calligraphers, but the text explicitly counts only "範、惇、達八人" as the 八絕, so those two are not among the eight [11].

## A point of inference

The *Wulu* list is the only place these eight are grouped together. Since Wu Fan, Liu Dun and Zhao Da all have their own chapter (*Wu Shu* 63), and the other five (Huang Xiang, Yan Wu, Song Shou, Cao Buxing, Zheng Yu) appear nowhere else in the *Sanguozhi* except this single Pei note, one can reasonably infer (this is inference) that the "eight excellences" grouping was a piece of local Wu lore that Pei Songzhi preserved from the *Wulu* rather than a formal roster in Chen Shou's main text.

q: In the Battle of Bowang, how did Zhuge Liang set the fire ambush against Xiahou Dun?
reply:
## Conclusion

In the *Sanguozhi*, the fire ambush at Bowang (博望) was **Liu Bei's (先主)** own stratagem, not Zhuge Liang's. Zhuge Liang is not mentioned in the Bowang engagement at all. The famous "Zhuge Liang burns Bowang Slope" (博望坡之火) is a *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* invention, not a recorded historical event.

## The actual record

**Liu Bei's own biography** describes the ambush:

「使拒夏侯惇、于禁等於博望。久之，先主設伏兵，一旦自燒屯偽遁，惇等追之，為伏兵所破。」[1]

(Liu Bei was sent to resist Xiahou Dun, Yu Jin and others at Bowang. After a long time, the Former Lord set an ambush; one morning he himself burned his camp and feigned flight; Dun and the others pursued, and were defeated by the ambush troops.)

**Li Dian's biography** gives more detail and names Li Dian's role as the voice of caution:

「劉表使劉備北侵，至葉，太祖遣典從夏侯惇拒之。備一旦燒屯去，惇率諸軍追擊之，典曰：『賊無故退，疑必有伏。南道狹窄，草木深，不可追也。』惇不聽，與於禁追之，典留守。惇等果入賊伏里，戰不利，典往救，備望見救至，乃散退。」[10]

(Liu Biao sent Liu Bei to invade north; when he reached Ye, the Grand Progenitor sent Li Dian to follow Xiahou Dun and resist him. One morning Bei burned his camp and left; Dun led all the armies in pursuit. Li Dian said: "The enemy withdraws without cause — I suspect there must be an ambush. The southern road is narrow, with deep grass and trees; we must not pursue." Dun did not listen, and pursued with Yu Jin, while Li Dian stayed to guard. Dun and the others indeed entered the enemy's ambush, fought at a disadvantage, and Li Dian went to their rescue; when Liu Bei saw the relief force arrive, he dispersed and withdrew.)

## The mechanism, as recorded

Putting the two accounts together, the ambush worked like this:

1. Liu Bei burned his own camp and pretended to flee [1][10].
2. Xiahou Dun took the bait and pursued into a narrow road with thick vegetation [10].
3. Li Dian warned that an unexplained retreat meant a likely ambush, but Xiahou Dun overrode him [10].
4. Xiahou Dun (with Yu Jin) entered the trap and was beaten; Li Dian came up with the reserve and rescued them, whereupon Liu Bei broke off and withdrew [1][10].

## Points of caution

- The commander of the ambush in the sources is **Liu Bei**; Li Dian is the one who saw through the trap, not Zhuge Liang. No source connects Zhuge Liang to this battle.
- The *Sanguozhi* text as I found it **does not give a year** for the Bowang engagement, so I will not assign one. (It is placed after Cao Cao's defeat of Yuan Shao and Liu Biao's reception of Liu Bei, but no explicit date is stated for the ambush itself.)

以下不是《三国志》的记载:

The story that Zhuge Liang devised the fire ambush at Bowang Slope — the "first exploit" of his career — is not in the *Sanguozhi*; it comes from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* or other non-orthodox accounts. In the *Sanguozhi* the stratagem is credited to Liu Bei himself.
